text:
In this exercise, you will construct the inverse of a matrix, a subject that we will investigate more fully in the next chapter. Suppose that $A$ is the $2\times2$ matrix: $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp -2 \\ -2 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right] $$ .

Find the vectors $\bvec_1$ and $\bvec_2$ such that the matrix $B=\left[\begin{array}{rr} \bvec_1 \amp \bvec_2 \end{array}\right]$ satisfies $$ AB = I = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right] $$ .

In general, it is not true that $AB = BA$. Check that it is true, however, for the specific $A$ and $B$ that appear in this problem.

Suppose that $\xvec = \twovec{x_1}{x_2}$. What do you find when you evaluate $I\xvec$?

Suppose that we want to solve the equation $A\xvec = \bvec$. We know how to do this using Gaussian elimination; let's use our matrix $B$ to find a different way: $$ \begin{aligned} A\xvec \amp {}={} \bvec \\ B(A\xvec) \amp {}={} B\bvec \\ (BA)\xvec \amp {}={} B\bvec \\ I\xvec \amp {}={} B\bvec \\ \xvec \amp {}={} B\bvec \\ \end{aligned} $$ . In other words, the solution to the equation $A\xvec=\bvec$ is $\xvec = B\bvec$.

Consider the equation $A\xvec = \twovec{5}{-2}$. Find the solution in two different ways, first using Gaussian elimination and then as $\xvec = B\bvec$, and verify that you have found the same result.
